1 Question & design

There is a confounder that has nothing to do with how divergent the sample is: where the reference itself is repetitive, a read cannot be uniquely placed. In such regions a 150 bp read fits several locations, bwa assigns low MAPQ, the MQ ≥ 20 filter drops it, and the variant there cannot be called — no matter how similar the sample is to the reference. This is the mechanism behind segmental-duplication / “difficult region” variant-calling failures, and it is a property of the reference, not the sample. (It is not something a sample-side duplication reproduces: a duplication of unique sequence still maps uniquely to the single reference copy — multi-mapping requires the reference to contain the repeat.)

We measure it directly with the real repeat structure of chr19:

  • Mappability (GenMap, K = 100, E = 2, computed on chr19 alone — reads are mapped to chr19 only, so mappability must be chr19-internal): value = 1 / (number of near-identical 100-mer copies within chr19). 1.0 = unique, 0.5 ≈ 2 copies, < 0.2 ≈ ≥ 5 copies. chr19 is 94.5 % unique; ~5.5 % is repetitive and 3.8 % is highly repetitive (< 0.2) — a minority of the genome, but a real one, and enriched for exactly the hard cases.
  • Recovery reuses the s01 SNP-only calls (homogeneous divergence D ∈ {0.02, 0.06, 0.10}, 30×, seed 42) so the divergence axis is clean. Each divergent SNP truth site is labeled with the mappability at its position and its recovery is scored per caller × divergence × iteration (scripts/mappability_recovery.py). Three bins: unique / repetitive / highly repetitive.
lev <- c("unique (1.0)", "repetitive (0.2-1.0)", "highly repetitive (<0.2)")
mr <- read_csv("analyses/s08-mappability/results/s08-mappability-recovery.csv") %>%
  mutate(caller = factor(caller, levels = c("gatk", "bcftools", "freebayes")),
         iteration = factor(iteration),
         divergence = as.numeric(divergence),
         map_bin = factor(map_bin, levels = lev))
mcols <- setNames(corecol(pal = "wilke", numcol = 3), lev)

2 Recovery falls with mappability, at every divergence

Single-shot (iteration 1) SNP recall against divergence, split by local mappability. The three lines separate at every divergence — the gap is already open at D = 0.02, where reference bias is otherwise mild — so this is a genuine mapping-ambiguity effect, not a divergence effect. And the two stack: the worst case is repetitive and divergent.

ggplot(mr %>% filter(iteration == "1"),
       aes(divergence, recall, color = map_bin)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = mcols, name = "reference\nmappability") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  facet_wrap(~caller, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "mean SNP divergence", y = "SNP recall (iteration 1)") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Interpretation. In unique sequence recall is at the reference-bias baseline (pileup callers ~100 % at low divergence). In highly repetitive sequence it is far lower — ~0.81 for the pileup callers even at D = 0.02, falling to ~0.65 at D = 0.10 — because the reads there are ambiguous and get filtered, before divergence even enters. gatk is lower throughout (its divergence sensitivity in unique sequence plus the mappability penalty), so repetitive + divergent sequence is where it collapses hardest (0.52 at D = 0.10). The mappability penalty and the divergence penalty are independent and additive.

3 Iteration relieves it — but only the divergence part

Unlike an SV breakpoint (a permanent blind spot), the mappability confounder is partly addressable by iteration. Comparing iteration 1 (dashed) to iteration 3 (solid):

ggplot(mr, aes(divergence, recall, color = map_bin, linetype = iteration)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = mcols, name = "reference\nmappability") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`1` = "dashed", `3` = "solid"), name = "iteration") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  facet_wrap(~caller, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "mean SNP divergence", y = "SNP recall") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Interpretation. Iteration lifts the repetitive curves substantially (bcftools highly-repetitive 0.81 → 0.95 at D = 0.02, 0.65 → 0.90 at D = 0.10). The reason is indirect: as the consensus absorbs recovered divergence, the effective divergence drops, so reads in semi-repetitive regions carry fewer mismatches and clear the MAPQ filter — the divergence-driven part of the ambiguity is relieved. But a residual repeat floor remains (highly-repetitive stays a few points below unique even at iteration 3), because a read that matches two identical copies is ambiguous regardless of divergence — that part iteration cannot touch.

4 Summary

  • A confounder independent of divergence. Where chr19 is repetitive, reads can’t be uniquely placed, get MAPQ-filtered, and the variant is lost — visible even at D = 0.02 (~19 pt in highly-repetitive sequence). It is a property of the reference, not the sample.
  • It stacks with divergence. Mappability and divergence penalties are independent and additive; repetitive + divergent sequence is the worst case (recall ~0.5–0.65 at D = 0.10).
  • Iteration helps partway. It relieves the divergence-driven portion (higher effective MAPQ) — bcftools highly-repetitive 0.65 → 0.90 — but leaves an irreducible repeat floor, because identical-copy ambiguity is divergence-independent.
  • Contrast with SVs (s07). An SV breakpoint is a permanent local blind spot iteration cannot touch; reference repetitiveness is a graded penalty iteration partly relieves. Both are read-placement failures outside the divergence axis — the two ways the map itself, not the sample, defeats recovery.
  • Scope. ~5.5 % of chr19 is affected — a minority, but the fraction where real variant calling is hardest, and the simulation analog of GIAB’s difficult-region stratification.

Data table + dictionary: results/s08-mappability-recovery.csv. GenMap K=100 E=2 on chr19; mappability at the SNP position. s01 SNP-only calls, seed 42.
